orders.title: WO-007 — Events, stores and data access for DotLn-Angular: the tiered event groups in `events`, NgRx SignalStore with the Events plugin, call state and the trinity through `data-access`, `BoardStore` behind `BoardFacade` loading the actor board over HTTP from the app's own API in the `uifa-board-v1` shape answered by MSW, the board's UI state persisted in browser storage, the app-tier stores for feature flags, navigation with canonical routes and errors in `state`, HTTP interceptors for base URL, timeouts and errors, MSW in development and in tests, and the action-hygiene check
orders.objective:
state in DotLn-Angular flows one way through typed events:
UI events dispatched by containers through facades, data-access events as
reusable commands with call state, navigation events resolved by one store
through canonical routes, app events for flags and errors; every event is
declared in `@dotln-angular/events` under its tier, the hygiene check counts
the exceptions, `BoardStore` loads the actor board (`uifa-board-v1`) through
HTTP from the app's own API (`GET <apiBaseUrl>/uifa-board-v1`), answered by
MSW in development and in tests, the board's own UI state (the selected
panel) persists in browser storage across reloads on the same origin,
nothing the app does writes outside the browser, and the shell shows the
error store's state.

**Observed gap (dated 2026-10-23, at the base `90fa6e8d`; restated by the
2026-10-24 pass):** no NgRx, no events, no HTTP and no mocks. `BoardFacade`
injects `BoardFixtureToken` (the recorded fixture
`libs/features/board/src/testing/fixtures/launchpad-board-2026-10-21.json`,
provided by `provideBoardFeature()` in `boardRoutes`), holds the selected
panel in a signal that is lost on reload, and owns `follow()`; the shell
(`apps/dotln/src/app/app.ts` over `DotlnAppLayout`) has no error surface;
`libs/shared/models` carries the `uifa-board-v1` types; the fixture's schema
copy was pinned from core's `main` at `a54f8d65` and the same bytes ship as a
kit file of the launchpad (starter v0.93.0 and v0.94.0); `nx.json` sets
`parallel` to 1 (WO-006-D025); the board's local anchors are bare fragments
(WO-006-D024). The operator decided on 2026-10-24 that the app is not wired
to core: its data comes from its own store through its own API, so the
platform resident's loopback is not read and the board's route is the app's
own, with `uifa-board-v1` kept as the response shape because the recorded
fixture and the kit schema already carry it. The Events plugin is stable
since NgRx 21 and `withEffects` is now `withEventHandlers`; the toolkit's
`withCallState` and `withStorageSync` exist for 22; MSW 3.x moved `http` and
`HttpResponse` to `msw/http`; `resource()` and `httpResource()` are stable
in Angular 22 (the 2026-10-18 planning document §4). The Angular builder
copies `public/` into every configuration's output unless a configuration
excludes a file, so the worker's exclusion from the production build is a
build-configuration matter, not a code path.

orders.title: WO-015 — The soldier scene: twenty units on a 2D canvas behind a renderer seam, a toolbox rail fed by the catalog, real-time-strategy selection, flock, arrive and a two-level formation with slot roles, a deterministic seeded clock, before-and-after trials, and the pure scene engine every later scene reuses
orders.objective:
at `/scene` the operator sees twenty units idling on a plain
field, each labelled with a lifecycle role; selects units as in a real-time
strategy game (click, shift-click, marquee, double-click for a squad, Escape
to clear, and the keyboard through the text layer); picks a tool from a rail
fed by the catalog (the ten movement and formation tools of the first scene
plus the catalog's first three tools per work, untyped ones shown as a
special case with a clarify affordance); reads its five faces and parameters
and sees the computed effect as ghost arrows before applying; applies flock,
arrive and a wedge, line or column formation with slot roles assigned from a
cost table; watches cohesion radius, collisions, heading variance, time to
objective and stalled units change in real time; compares the branch before
and after an equip with the first divergence marked; saves compositions that
survive a reload; and nothing leaves the browser. The same seed and the same
steps reproduce the same frames; under reduced motion the field is still
until Step or Play; the canvas is a projection of a frame the text layer also
renders, and the renderer sits behind one interface so a 3D painter can
replace it later without touching the engine.

goalReview.goalStandard:
## Goal-aligned decisions

The [sequence](../planning/sequence.md) and selected work order determine
current placement and authority. The mission is the outcome; the critical path
is the dependency route to the next outcome. Useful prerequisite or
risk-reduction work must name the blocked outcome it enables. Process activity,
receipt volume and agent utilization are not progress by themselves. Goal
alignment grants no authority to reorder or expand work. In all phases, the Goal
Alignment and Process Cost procedure lives in the generated role skills
[WO-043, 2026-09-11].

Accuracy takes priority over agreement in every phase. The already-equipped
Correctness over Sycophancy rule applies to operator suggestions and the agent's
own premises equally: challenge unsupported claims, distinguish observation
from inference, state material uncertainty, and correct mistakes when evidence
changes. A confident request or an earlier decision is not proof of correctness.
Record material disagreement and its evidence in the same decision or phase
receipt; do not manufacture dissent or seek approval for ordinary judgment.

| Lens                                  | Decision question                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Policy resistance / fixes that fail   | Will local goals or guards undo one another?                                                              |
| Tragedy of the commons                | Does the solution consume shared compute, context or operator attention without accounting for the total? |
| Drift to low performance              | Does it improve an explicit outcome standard rather than normalize a worse baseline?                      |
| Escalation                            | Will additional process provoke more process or workarounds?                                              |
| Success to the successful             | Are credible alternatives excluded merely because the current mechanism already has investment?           |
| Shifting the burden to the intervenor | Does the solution remove recurring operator rescue or depend on it?                                       |
| Rule beating                          | Can the evidence pass without the intended behavior occurring?                                            |
| Seeking the wrong goal                | Does it advance operator flow and the selected product outcome rather than a proxy?                       |

Naive Interventionism adds the existing system's useful functions, affected
consumers, second-order harm, reversibility and smallest useful probe. NoOp
records what happens if nothing changes, why action or inaction wins, and the
evidence that would reopen the choice. Scale detail to consequence: explain
applicable risks and briefly group immaterial lenses with a reason; do not
manufacture eight repetitive paragraphs for routine edits.

Record evidence of benefit and the risks of intervening in existing behavior;
verification and handoff compare observed outcomes with the promised benefit.
Required legal or release actions retain their existing authority; NoOp is a
considered alternative, not an ambient veto or permission to abandon authorized
work.



Material choices and rationales go in existing phase evidence: per-order
`docs/evidence/WO-NNN/decisions.md` and cited product sections for work-order
decisions; planning dispositions/candidate records for planning choices; the
independent report or refutation receipt for its judgment; retained closeout
evidence for release decisions. The decisions index exposes per-order records.
Reuse and link a current rationale until its assumptions change; do not create
a parallel decision log or an extra approval ritual.


This launchpad is the operator's own DotLn instance. Its purpose is to plan and
run bounded, evidence-gated work orders across the operator's repositories, so
that every change arrives as a pull request the operator reads before it merges,
while the kit itself stays upstream and reaches this fork only through starter
updates. The first workstream is DotLn-Angular, an Nx and Angular monorepo that
serves two outcomes at once: the operator's reference Angular workspace, which a
colleague should recognize as the way the operator builds Angular, and the
operator's sandbox app, one app with sub-apps behind a menu: a scene for
authoring game AI from a toolbox mined from the works the operator reads, a
view of DotLn's machinery where a change to an agent's mechanisms shows what
changes in an example use case, the operator's own digital twin, and side
utilities. Every new idea lives there first as a toy the operator plays with
before promoting the ones that work, for the five UIFA roles, people and
software actors alike. The app is not wired to DotLn core: its data comes from
public mining into its own store, served to the UI through its own API, and it
informs the platform through GitHub issues, never by writing a control record,
so that the app improves the platform, the platform the starter, the starter
this fork, and the fork the app in turn. The critical path runs from registering
that repository in this launchpad, through one witnessed target order that
scaffolds the workspace, to a foundation where a feature is added by convention:
shared libraries, the component taxonomy, events and stores, the sub-app shell,
and a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model. Later
workstreams join the same way: one registration and one planning pass each,
with the fork's own machinery changes cut as self orders beside them.

findings.reason: The worker plan has no slack. Eight classifiers, two sampling checkers, one synthesizer and one critic make twelve, which is exactly the cap criterion 5 enforces. Step 7 requires rerunning the classifier on every failing id a checker returns. A rerun spawned as a new worker makes thirteen and fails criterion 5. That pushes the executor to skip reruns, or to resume workers in a way the evidence README does not record separately.
findings.reopenWhen: Either sampling checker returns at least one failing id, or the evidence README lists a rerun dispatch.

findings.reason: Criterion 3 is a quota: three tools with a closed-enum transform for each of six works, including PoEAA, GEB and Team Topologies. The enum's fourteen kinds cover steering, formation, squads, channels, ground and levels. The criterion can pass by force-fitting a transform onto a concept that has none. The only counter-pressure is the checkers' sample asking whether the transform is observable in a twenty-unit scene, and WO-015's rail then presents those tools as executable.
findings.reopenWhen: A checker or the critic disputes any of the eighteen first-three tools, or a work's first three carry a transform kind that WO-015's engine does not interpret.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: not a foundation element. It is the first sub-app the vision names ('a scene for authoring game AI') and the operator's first playable toy. In this horizon no order depends on it: WO-016 depends on WO-013 only, and WO-015 precedes it only by sequence and base. NoOp in the records: metrics null. The NoOp state is /scene as WO-013's arriving page. If nothing changes, the sandbox has no toy and the catalog has no consumer that executes a tool. Action wins on the mission, since this is the vision's first outcome, not on the critical path.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: it reuses WO-007's withPersistedState as the single storage path. It admits a canvas-owning wrapper by adding one taxonomy sentence rather than by bypassing the component lint. No guard is fought. Tragedy of the commons: about 70 files, 8 to 12 hours and about 180 KB of context, plus an e2e spec with axe at three widths that every later gate reruns; no dependency is added. Drift to low performance: none observed; determinism and a hand-computed slot table raise the standard. Escalation: not material; it adds a fixture check into check:fixtures. Success to the successful: Babylon.js now, SVG, per-role behaviours and randomness by default are each rejected with an axis, and the renderer seam keeps the 3D alternative open. Shifting the burden: if a needed tool arrives untyped, the executor types it with a recorded decision rather than escalating; no operator rescue. Rule beating: the criteria are behavioral: identical frame hashes over 600 frames, collisions with separation off, a hand-computed slot assignment, first divergence at the equip frame plus one, and at most one vm change per frame. trial-known-outcome.json is generated by the engine's own spec, which makes it a change detector, but it is not a criterion. Seeking the wrong goal: the rail lists three tools per work from works whose transform kinds the engine does not interpret, and Apply has no defined behavior for them (finding). The virtual-time clock is called shared before the library it claims to share with exists (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes WO-013's arriving page for /scene. It adds about 70 source files, an engine library, a data-access library, four fixtures, a check and two documents. Net additive by design.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly degrades. A storage failure falls back to WO-007's in-memory default. Under reduced motion the field stays still until Step or Play. An untyped tool opens clarify and never executes. The text layer renders the same frame as the canvas, so a canvas failure still leaves a usable surface. Unspecified: a typed tool whose TransformKind the interpreter lacks (nine of the fourteen kinds) has no declared refusal, no-op or error state.

findings.reason: The rail lists the catalog's first three tools for each of six works. The engine design covers only five transform kinds (steer.blend, steer.priority, formation.twoLevel, formation.fixed, objective.set), and its non-goals exclude channels, influence maps, a commander and pathfinding. No interpreter is named for the other nine TransformKind members. The order defines what an untyped tool does (opens clarify, never executes) but not what happens to a typed tool whose kind the interpreter lacks: Apply has no declared refusal, no-op or error state.
findings.reopenWhen: Any firstThree tool's transform kind lies outside the five the engine implements, and Apply on it does not show a visible refusal with its reason.

findings.reason: SceneClock's RxJS virtual-time driver is described as 'shared with WO-016's replay'. But WO-016 runs after this order and creates libs/shared/replay itself, and WO-013's convention puts clocks that every sub-app reads under libs/shared/. So either two virtual-time clocks exist after WO-016, or WO-016 must refactor this order's clock, and neither order plans that. The dependency direction is inverted.
findings.reopenWhen: After WO-016 merges, SceneClock's virtual driver and ReplayClock both exist with separate virtual-scheduler code.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: not a foundation element. It is the vision's machinery view ('a change to an agent's mechanisms shows what changes in an example use case'). It unblocks WO-017 (hard: the records fold, the replay clock and the menu group). NoOp in the records: metrics null. It reconciles the conflict explicitly: the criterion 6 exception, production ideaSinkUrl null, loopback only, a 16 KB cap and a non-loopback refusal test. The sink lives under tools/, outside WO-007's Node-import grep. Tragedy of the commons: about 75 files, 8 to 12 hours and about 190 KB, plus a long-running local process the operator must start beside nx serve. Drift to low performance: the fixtures are a named stopgap, with a stated path to become a route or be deleted once C1 exists. Escalation: two new checks (record fixtures, sink tooling) and one command. Success to the successful: live loopback, generated cards, drag and episodes are each rejected on the operator's decisions. Shifting the burden: ideas are saved only when the operator runs the sink, and a failed post is one toast that never blocks; acceptable. Rule beating: the material trap here. Only addWait has a defined effect on the use case's beats, so criterion 7 and step 10 pass when a mechanism change redraws the agent's card and leaves the example use case unchanged (finding). The counts are true at the base: the six Origin stamps carry 19, 13, 13, 13, 13 and 13 ids. 'Scene' is also overloaded across ConcertScene and scene-reader in records, the scene sub-app and its engine, and SceneTypeId in the catalog (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes WO-013's arriving page for /machinery. It adds about 75 files, two shared libraries, a data-access library, a Node process, a reducer, a check, three fixtures and two documents.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades. If the sink fails, the operator gets one toast and the drop proceeds. An unknown event type becomes an unknown beat and is never dropped. A refused drop stays visible with its reason and leaves the scene unchanged. A storage failure falls back to WO-007's default. The reducer prints PASS or FAIL without values and the fixture check fails closed, which is correct for provenance.

findings.reason: The vision passage describes the machinery view as one 'where a change to an agent's mechanisms shows what changes in an example use case'. Here applyIdeas is a pure fold, and no model links a gem, support, knowledge, rung or prose change to the beats; only addWait has a defined effect on the use case. Step 10's check (the card's mechanism count falls while the ghost keeps the before) and criterion 7 (an idea redrawn with the ghost and the presentation-only band) both pass with the example use case unchanged. The evidence can pass without the intended behavior occurring.
findings.reopenWhen: The facade spec or e2e shows an applied idea other than addWait whose beats are identical before and after, or the operator reports that a mechanism change shows no change in the use case.

findings.reason: Criterion 3 hard-codes starter v0.94.0 and the stamp counts: 19 for the executor and 13 for each other role. Both hold at the base: the six Origin stamps carry 19, 13, 13, 13, 13 and 13 ids, and UPSTREAM.md names v0.94.0. But WO-016 is sixth in a serial chain and recent orders have taken the starter repeatedly, so a starter update before activation would make the criterion false or force a copy of stale data.
findings.reopenWhen: When WO-016 activates, UPSTREAM.md's tag differs from v0.94.0, or any role stamp's id count differs from 19 or 13.

findings.reason: 'Scene' is overloaded. The records library gains scene-reader.ts and ConcertScene for control segments; WO-015 owns the scene sub-app, with SceneDefinition and SceneFrame in scene-engine; the catalog types SceneTypeId. Three unrelated meanings in shared libraries add naming confusion for every later sub-app and session that reads them.
findings.reopenWhen: A later order imports from both scene-engine and records and has to alias a Scene name, or a review finds a Scene type used across the two meanings.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: The final foundation step ('a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model'). WS-001 is delivered when WO-004 to WO-008 merge, and this order unblocks the unfiled DotLn console feature the goal standard names as the product purpose. Its gates are WO-007's merge, the base-reset planning pass and the starter `--draft` gate. NoOp in the records: the row's metrics are null. NoOp leaves WS-001 undelivered.
orders.systemTraps: Rule beating (material): criterion 1's storage scan asserts that no stored value matches the JWT shape, so an opaque refresh or access token written to storage by the client library passes, and 'holds tokens only in memory' goes unproved for non-JWT tokens. The mock knows every token it issues and could assert that none appears in storage. The objective's 'swapping the mocked provider for a real one changes configuration and nothing in the Angular code' is documented (criterion 6) but no criterion exercises a second provider configuration. Policy resistance and secrets: the Cost line commits a development signing key to a public repository. A development key is not a credential to any real system, but it matches the private-key patterns forge secret scanning looks for: it can raise an alert and, where push protection covers the pattern, refuse the publish. Generating the key pair when the mock starts (jose) avoids committing it. Criterion 5 keeps the kid out of the production bundle but not out of the repository. Tragedy of the commons: the largest order (about 160 KB, 8 to 12 hours, 15 steps; tokens unknown), and the record shows 1 of the last 3 orders failed first verification (WO-003), so size raises re-verification exposure. Escalation, drift, success to the successful, shifting the burden and seeking the wrong goal are immaterial: no new commands, a stricter failure matrix, the client library is chosen at activation, no operator step is added, and the work is the product.
orders.removalBalance: No. It says 'Removes nothing' and adds libs/shared/auth with its kit, the mocked provider's handlers and key, two event groups, guards, a permission directive, two routes, about 60 files and two dependencies.
orders.failureBehavior: Fails toward safety by design: refresh failure and invalid tokens sign the user out, and a denied route redirects to /denied (criteria 3 and 4). Session loss on reload, from memory-only tokens, leads to a new sign-in through the provider rather than an error. The mock is excluded from production (criterion 5), and an unreachable real provider leads to /login. One failure refuses rather than degrades: committed private-key material can be refused by forge secret scanning when the branch is published.

findings.reason: The JWT-shape storage assertion misses opaque tokens, so a stored non-JWT refresh token passes. Comparing storage values with the tokens the mock issued would prove the memory-only rule.
findings.reopenWhen: The mocked provider or the chosen client library issues or stores a non-JWT token, or a storage value after sign-in equals a token the mock issued, while criterion 1's assertion passes.

findings.reason: The provider-swap property is stated in documentation but never exercised, so its evidence can pass without the behavior.
findings.reopenWhen: The first real identity provider configuration, in the later example-API member, requires a change to any file under libs/ or apps/ other than environment files.

findings.reason: A committed development signing key puts private-key material in a public repository, where secret scanning can flag it or refuse the push. Generating the key when the mock starts removes the material.
findings.reopenWhen: After WO-008, a tracked DotLn-Angular file contains a PEM private-key block or a JWK with a private `d` member, or a secret-scanning alert or push refusal is raised on WO-008's branch.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: not a foundation element. It is the vision's 'operator's own digital twin'. No order depends on it functionally; WO-018 depends on it only as the serial base. NoOp in the records: metrics null. The NoOp state is that the app has no model of the operator. If nothing changes, the twin stays a design in intake. Its hard dependency on WO-008 is serial position only, so auth, the last foundation element, precedes it by sequence, which is consistent with the order the vision gives.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: it lands after WO-008, whose routePermissions is a Record over BasePaths with a spec asserting full coverage. Yet WO-017 adds BasePaths.Twin and names neither a permission nor a signed-in e2e path (finding). Tragedy of the commons: about 55 files, 6 to 9 hours and about 170 KB. The variant registry only grows, since by decision a variant is never deleted, so the picker and the check grow without bound by design. Drift to low performance: replacing the design's fidelity cell with results is the operator's decision; the order states that one order's seven gaps are a toy sample and claims nothing beyond it. Escalation: two commands and a check that reads git history. Success to the successful: RxJS as the model is the operator's decision, and an interpreted JSON model is rejected. Credible. Shifting the burden: none on the happy path. Kept flips are exported TypeScript that the operator commits by hand, which is an intended operator action. Rule beating: criterion 2's 'a flip changes the twin's figures' passes trivially, and criterion 3's grep only bans words. The material issue is the result fold itself, under the next lens. Seeking the wrong goal: the fold replays recorded worker durations and verdicts after each dispatch, and early fires are zero by construction. A variant with every duration at zero therefore dominates on all three figures (close about 883.3 minutes, 0 waiting, 0 early fires), so 'judged by results' rewards modelling no one (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes nothing. It adds about 55 files, a model library with three variants, a registry that by rule never shrinks, two scripts and commands, a feature and two documents.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades in the browser: the presence variant is shown locked, the size multiplier reads unknown, and WO-016's resolution parameter hedges the scheduler choice. Unspecified at the tooling edge: twin:check reads the base manifest with git show, and the order does not say whether the check fails or passes vacuously when the base commit is absent, as in a shallow CI clone.

findings.reason: The result fold replays the recorded worker durations and verdicts after each twin dispatch. So the order's outcome does not depend on the twin's timing, and early fires are zero by construction for any variant that fires after a hand-back. A flip that sets every patience-table duration to zero therefore yields a virtual close of about 883.3 minutes (1,110.3 minus 227.0), zero waiting minutes and zero early fires. That is the best value on all three figures from a variant that models no one. Judged by results alone, the cell cannot tell a faithful twin from a trivial one. The results-only rule is the operator's decision, so this is a constructible counterexample, not a hold.
findings.reopenWhen: A zero-duration or all-minimum flip scores best on all three figures in the twin-model spec or the e2e, or the operator keeps a variant whose durations are all below the recorded gaps.

findings.reason: WO-017 adds BasePaths.Twin on a base where WO-008's guards are live and its routePermissions is a Record over BasePaths, with a spec asserting that the keys equal the enum. Yet WO-017's design, steps and e2e name no permission for /twin and no signed-in path. The build or WO-008's spec will force an unplanned permission decision in the middle of execution.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-017's build or WO-008's routePermissions spec fails on the new member, or the /twin e2e is redirected to /login or /denied.

findings.reason: twin:check reads the base manifest with git show <base>. In a shallow CI checkout the base commit may be missing, and the order does not say whether a missing base fails the check or passes it vacuously. A vacuous pass would let a deleted variant through and defeat the never-deleted rule.
findings.reopenWhen: twin:check runs where the base commit has not been fetched, or its tooling test does not cover the missing-base case.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: not a foundation element. It is the vision's 'public mining into its own store': the first map the app owns, plus a toy shelf. It unblocks nothing in this horizon; it is the last member, and the commander scene and toy builds are candidates. NoOp in the records: metrics null. The NoOp state is no Art of War rows, no toy record type and no shelf. If nothing changes, the catalog keeps six works and the run's placeholders stay. The title's 'app's own store' is committed JSON in a library. The mining store and its API (candidate C1) remain absent, so this horizon never reaches the vision's 'served to the UI through its own API'.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the material trap here. Its map rows carry exactly the fields WO-014's allow-list refuses, in the directory WO-014's grep scans, and its toy-source tools break WO-014's tool-v0 shape (findings). Tragedy of the commons: two fan-outs totalling twelve workers, exactly the cap, with no slack for the rewrite the critic triggers (finding). Tokens are unknown until run and recorded per worker, and the public text is fetched once over the network. Drift to low performance: none of the 25 toys is playable at close, so the shelf is a backlog rendered as product. Acceptable as the operator's stated way to pick the next toy. Escalation: two new checks (check-map, toys:check), negative fixtures and rules; none retired. Success to the successful: it reuses WO-014's brief and merge script instead of inventing a second pipeline. Credible. Shifting the burden: the operator picks the next toy from the shelf, which is intended. Rule beating: 'never a passage' is enforced only by a 240-character bound and a twenty-row critic sample, even though the fetched text is available for a mechanical overlap check (finding). Seeking the wrong goal: adding a seventh work and toy-source tools runs into earlier orders' 'six works' assertions, with no plan to update them or to regenerate catalog-summary.json (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes nothing. It adds two catalog files, a schema, a model, toys.json, toy-source tool files, a page, two checks, a command and new document sections: about 30 files and 300 rows.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly refuses where it should. A toy naming an unknown tool id fails toys:check, and a definition over 240 characters fails check-map. A transform kind the enum lacks becomes untyped with the proposed kind in its reason, which degrades rather than refuses. Unspecified: a failed fetch of the public text blocks the map pass with no named fallback, and the interaction with WO-014's check is not stated, so the likely first failure is catalog:check refusing the new map file.

findings.reason: WO-018 writes libs/shared/catalog/src/data/map-artofwar.json with definition, related, verified, chapter and section fields. WO-014's check-catalog refuses rows carrying those fields, WO-014 criterion 2's grep over that same directory must print nothing, and WO-014's rules say the commit carries only ids, short titles and generic terms. WO-018 says catalog:check 'already covers the new files' and names no change to the check's scope or to that rule. The two orders' guards conflict, and the likely first failure is catalog:check refusing the new map.
findings.reopenWhen: catalog:check or WO-014's criterion-2 grep fails with map-artofwar.json present, or the executor narrows check-catalog's scope without a recorded decision.

findings.reason: WO-014's Tool requires map { file, line, sha256 }, ids of the form <slug>:<line> and additionalProperties false, and its check requires the tool row count to equal the maps' total in the summary. WO-018's toy-source tools carry map null and provenance 'public-work' and have no map rows. They therefore fail tool-v0 and the count rule unless the schema, the id rule and the count rule change, and none of those changes is planned.
findings.reopenWhen: tool-v0 validation refuses a tools-<source>.json file, or the summary's row-count rule fails after the toy-source tools merge.

findings.reason: WO-014 criterion 3 and WO-015 criterion 4 both assert 'six works'. WO-018 adds a seventh work (artofwar, with three typed tools per its criterion 2) and toy-source tools. Its synthesizer writes only toys-summary.json, so no step regenerates catalog-summary.json or updates the scene rail's assertions. Yet WO-018's gate runs the whole e2e suite, and catalog:report must list artofwar.
findings.reopenWhen: The scene e2e or the catalog-summary spec fails in WO-018's gate, or catalog:report lists artofwar without a recorded regeneration of catalog-summary.json.

findings.reason: 'Never a passage' is enforced only by a 240-character bound and a twenty-row critic sample. The fetched public text sits in the session scratch with a recorded SHA-256, yet no mechanical overlap check compares the definitions against it. A verbatim passage under 240 characters therefore passes check-map.
findings.reopenWhen: A word-run overlap check of map-artofwar.json against the recorded text finds a definition sharing a long run of consecutive words with it.

findings.reason: Two mappers, one map critic, one classifier, six designers, one synthesizer and one critic make twelve, exactly the cap criterion 4 enforces. The mapper rewrites the rows the map critic names, so a respawned mapper makes thirteen. This is the same zero-slack shape as WO-014.
findings.reopenWhen: The map critic names at least one row and the rewrite is dispatched as a new worker.
